1: Her only solo studio album, blending soul, reggae and hip-hop, featuring "Doo Wop (That Thing)" and winning five Grammys including Album of the Year.
2: Produced by Quincy Jones, it yielded seven Top 10 singles, among them "Billie Jean" and "Beat It", and became the best-selling album ever.
3: The last album the band recorded together, closing with a long side-two medley and opening with "Come Together"; its zebra-crossing cover is widely imitated.
4: Soundtrack to his film of the same name, recorded with the Revolution, featuring "When Doves Cry" and the title ballad, partly recorded live in Minneapolis.
5: Spare, guitar-and-keyboard-driven songs like "Nikes" and "Self Control", released independently a day after the visual album Endless.
6: A sprawling double LP with a bonus EP, featuring "Sir Duke", "Isn't She Lovely" and "As", topping the US chart for fourteen weeks.
7: Subtitled "a short film", it traces a teenage day in Compton through skits and songs like "Swimming Pools" and "Money Trees".
8: Made with Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi, the Dap-Kings backing much of it, it recasts sixties girl-group soul around heartbreak, led by "Rehab".
9: Produced by Butch Vig, it carried "Smells Like Teen Spirit" to the mainstream and knocked Michael Jackson's Dangerous from the top of Billboard.
10: Released with an hour-long film, it confronts infidelity and Black womanhood across tracks like "Formation" and "Hold Up".
11: Written amid the band members' breakups, it includes "Dreams", "Go Your Own Way" and "The Chain", and spent 31 weeks at number one.
12: Recorded partly in actress Jane Seymour's mansion, it explores technology and alienation through songs like "Paranoid Android" and "Karma Police".
13: Built on soul samples by Kanye West and Just Blaze, it includes "Izzo (H.O.V.A.)" and "Takeover", and was released on September 11.
14: Opens with the six-minute "Like a Rolling Stone" and closes with "Desolation Row", eleven minutes of surreal acoustic storytelling.
15: A breakup record anchored by "Rolling in the Deep" and "Someone Like You", it won Album of the Year at the Grammys.
16: Spare confessional songs played on piano, dulcimer and guitar, including "A Case of You", "River" and "California".
17: A song cycle told from a returning Vietnam veteran's view, addressing war, poverty and ecology, with tracks flowing seamlessly into one another.
18: A re-recording of her synth-heavy 2014 album, adding five previously unreleased "From the Vault" tracks like "Is It Over Now?".
19: Introduced G-funk's slow, Parliament-sampling grooves and showcased Snoop Doggy Dogg on "Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang".
20: Brian Wilson's studio-crafted song cycle with harpsichord, bicycle bells and barking dogs, featuring "God Only Knows" and "Wouldn't It Be Nice".
21: Studio experiments with tape loops, backwards guitar and Indian instrumentation, closing with the swirling "Tomorrow Never Knows".
22: Wall of Sound-inspired production, Clarence Clemons's saxophone and the title track's escape fantasy made it Springsteen's commercial breakthrough.
23: Filtered disco and house samples, vocoder vocals and "One More Time" anchor a record paired with the anime film Interstella 5555.
24: Concept album about an alien rock star, featuring guitarist Mick Ronson and songs like "Starman" and "Suffragette City".
25: Built on modal scales and recorded in two sessions with John Coltrane and Bill Evans, it's among the best-selling jazz records ever.
26: Maximalist production recorded largely in Hawaii, with "Runaway" and "Power" and guests including Nicki Minaj, Rick Ross and Bon Iver.
27: Recorded piecemeal while touring, it opens with "Whole Lotta Love" and features John Bonham's drum showcase "Moby Dick".
28: Heartbeats, cash-register loops and Clare Torry's wordless vocals on "The Great Gig in the Sky" frame meditations on time, money and madness.
29: Fuses jazz basslines, including Ron Carter on one track, with sparse beats, ending with the posse cut "Scenario" featuring Busta Rhymes.
30: Recorded in Finneas O'Connell's small Los Angeles bedroom studio, its whispered vocals and booming bass drive "Bad Guy".
31: Co-written with Glen Ballard, its raw confessional rock includes "Ironic" and "You Oughta Know", which features Flea on bass.
32: Debut blending street narratives with radio hits "Juicy" and "Big Poppa", executive produced by Sean Combs for Bad Boy Records.
33: Swapped guitars for synthesizers, drum machines and processed vocals influenced by Warp Records electronica, opening with "Everything in Its Right Place".
34: The Bomb Squad's dense, sample-stacked sirens and noise underpin Chuck D's politics on tracks like "Don't Believe the Hype".
35: Double album mixing punk with reggae, ska, rockabilly and R&B; its cover shows Paul Simonon smashing his bass onstage.
36: Released without warning on iTunes as a "visual album" with a video for every song, including "Drunk in Love".
37: RZA's grimy, kung fu film-sampling production backs nine rappers trading verses on tracks including "C.R.E.A.M." and "Protect Ya Neck".
38: Piano-led songs including "It's Too Late" and "You've Got a Friend", plus her own versions of hits she'd written for others.
39: Queensbridge debut with production from DJ Premier, Pete Rock, Q-Tip and Large Professor, featuring "N.Y. State of Mind".
40: Her Atlantic debut, partly recorded at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, opens with her commanding version of Otis Redding's "Respect".
41: Third Outkast record, blending Southern funk, live instrumentation and cosmic storytelling, with the harmonica breakdown of "Rosa Parks" and "Da Art of Storytellin'".
42: Her first collaboration with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, built on hard Minneapolis funk drum machines and declaring independence from her family.
43: Brian Eno-produced record built from layered, looped polyrhythms inspired by Fela Kuti, featuring the chanted, sermon-like "Once in a Lifetime".
44: Largely self-played on synthesizers and keyboards, tackling drug addiction and urban poverty on "Living for the City" and "Higher Ground".
45: Pairs lush string arrangements with harsh electronic beats, conceived as a portrait of Iceland's volcanic landscape, including "Jóga" and "Bachelorette".
46: Recorded in London after Marley survived an assassination attempt in Jamaica, featuring "Jamming", "Three Little Birds" and "One Love/People Get Ready".
47: Moody, nocturnal second record largely produced by Noah "40" Shebib, featuring the Rihanna duet title track and "Marvins Room".
48: Dense sample collage produced with the Dust Brothers, stitching hundreds of fragments from funk, rock and soul records into intricate tracks.
49: Steeped in fascination with America's landscapes and mythology, opening with "Where the Streets Have No Name" and containing "With or Without You".
50: Side one holds singles like "Running Up That Hill"; side two is "The Ninth Wave", a suite about a woman adrift at sea.
51: Sprawling double album assembled from abandoned projects, mixing funk, gospel and rock, with the stark, drum-machine-driven title track about social ills.
52: Raw, sleazy debut about Los Angeles street life, featuring Slash's guitar riffs on "Sweet Child o' Mine" and "Welcome to the Jungle".
53: Double album largely recorded in the basement of Keith Richards' rented French villa, a murky mix of blues, country, soul and gospel.
54: Four-part spiritual suite recorded in a single session with his classic quartet, opening with a chanted "a love supreme" refrain.
55: Loose, moody departure from her radio hits, mixing dancehall single "Work" with soul, psychedelia and a Tame Impala cover.
56: Slow, enveloping wall of guitars and keyboards from a gloomy Robert Smith, including the singles "Lovesong", "Pictures of You" and "Lullaby".
57: Loose, live-feeling neo-soul grooves cut at Electric Lady Studios with Questlove and the Soulquarians, including "Untitled (How Does It Feel)".
58: Second Oasis record, packed with anthemic Britpop singalongs like "Wonderwall" and "Don't Look Back in Anger", written by Noel Gallagher.
59: Slinky, late-night record fusing hip-hop-style beats with heavy rock riffs and falsetto backing vocals, featuring "Do I Wanna Know?" and "R U Mine?"
60: Debut with Andy Warhol's peeled-banana cover, documenting drugs and street life on "Heroin" and "I'm Waiting for the Man", mostly sung by Lou Reed.
61: Sade's fourth record, a hushed, minimal set of slow-burning grooves featuring "No Ordinary Love" and "Cherish the Day".
62: A double album, the first released on Death Row after his prison release, featuring "California Love" and "Ambitionz Az a Ridah".
63: Debut by the Experience trio, introducing feedback-drenched guitar on "Purple Haze", "Foxy Lady" and the backward-tape experiment "Are You Experienced?".
64: Debut that helped define neo soul, pairing jazz-tinged grooves with Badu's Billie Holiday-like phrasing on the single "On & On".
65: Playful debut produced by Prince Paul, built from dense, eclectic samples, with skits and the single "Me Myself and I".
66: Third studio album, setting Morrissey's wit and melancholy against Johnny Marr's guitars on "There Is a Light That Never Goes Out".
67: Bristol trio's debut, setting Beth Gibbons's aching vocals over scratchy samples and spy-film atmospherics on "Glory Box" and "Sour Times".
68: Debut of lean, scratchy guitar songs recorded in New York, whose terse sound fueled a garage rock revival, including "Last Nite".
69: Third album and the last with bassist Cliff Burton, built around the long, shifting title track and the instrumental "Orion".
70: Ruthless Records debut whose title track and "Fuck tha Police" brought Los Angeles gangsta rap to national attention and FBI scrutiny.
71: Train journeys across Europe inspire motorik rhythms and cool synthesizer melodies, later sampled for Afrika Bambaataa's "Planet Rock".
72: Long-awaited second album of candid heartbreak and revenge fantasies, spanning R&B, pop-punk and hip-hop, featuring the hit "Kill Bill".
73: Polished jazz-inflected recordings using elite session players, including Wayne Shorter's saxophone solo and Steve Gadd's drumming on the title track.
74: Industrial concept album tracing a man's self-destruction, recorded in the house where the Manson murders occurred, closing with "Hurt".
75: Debut produced with Timbaland, whose skittering, spacious beats shaped late-nineties sound, led by "The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)".
76: Caribbean summer record moving through reggaeton, dembow, bachata and mambo, with hits like "Me Porto Bonito" and "Tití Me Preguntó".
77: Personal record touching on her Catholic upbringing and family, whose title track and video sparked controversy and lost a Pepsi deal.
78: Sprawling double album written with Bernie Taupin, containing "Bennie and the Jets", "Candle in the Wind" and "Funeral for a Friend".
79: Largely co-produced with Jack Antonoff, this piano-led record offers a hazy portrait of California, from the title track to "Venice Bitch".
80: Fast-selling, provocative record answering critics and fame through characters like Slim Shady, featuring "Stan", "The Real Slim Shady" and "The Way I Am".
81: Recorded partly in Young's Topanga Canyon basement with teenage Nils Lofgren on piano, featuring "Southern Man" and the dreamlike title song.
82: Debut executive-produced by Dr. Dre and Eminem, propelled by the Dr. Dre-produced club hit "In da Club".
83: Debut produced by John Cale, opening with a reworked "Gloria" and fusing beat poetry with raw garage rock.
84: Debut produced by Dr. Dre on Death Row Records, built on slow G-funk grooves and anchored by "Gin and Juice".
85: Co-produced with Daniel Tashian and Ian Fitchuk, blending disco, soft rock and banjo; it won the Grammy for Album of the Year.
86: Deeply personal second record drawing on depression and a turbulent relationship, built on 1970s soul samples with Sean "Puffy" Combs producing.
87: Bristol collective's debut, blending slow hip-hop beats, dub basslines and soul vocals, with Shara Nelson singing the string-swept "Unfinished Sympathy".
88: Philips release pairing Simone's brooding take on Screamin' Jay Hawkins's title track with orchestral arrangements and her version of "Feeling Good".
89: Eight-song expansion of The Fame exploring darker themes of fear, featuring "Bad Romance", "Telephone" with Beyoncé, and "Alejandro".
90: First record with singer Brian Johnson after Bon Scott's death, opening with tolling "Hells Bells" and dressed in an all-black mourning cover.
91: Introspective follow-up to Faith, promoted without Michael in its videos; supermodels lip-sync in his place in "Freedom! '90".
92: Lush, jazz-tinged production with strings and synths frames lyrics about loneliness and sexuality, on songs like "See You Again" and "Garden Shed".
93: Spare, airy R&B exploring Black identity and grief, threaded with spoken interludes from her parents and Master P, including "Cranes in the Sky".
94: Crackling vinyl hiss, pitch-shifted vocal fragments and shuffling UK garage beats, assembled by William Bevan using the basic audio editor Sound Forge.
95: Blockbuster R&B record featuring the Lil Jon-produced crunk smash "Yeah!" and confessional ballads like "Burn", with lyrics hinting at personal infidelity.
96: Debut written with producer Joel Little when she was a teenager in Auckland, built on sparse beats and the hit "Royals".
97: Debut fusing Zack de la Rocha's political rap with Tom Morello's turntable-like guitar effects, including "Killing in the Name".
98: Named after a demolished Houston theme park, packed with guest artists and featuring the multi-part, beat-switching hit "Sicko Mode" with Drake.
99: Joe Walsh's first album with the band, exploring California excess; the title track ends with a long dual guitar solo by Don Felder and Walsh.
100: Gathers songs from her three 2010 Body Talk mini-albums, pairing icy electropop with heartbreak, including "Dancing On My Own".
